# SK2171 — The `\x` escape's length is decided by what follows it

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `\x` escape in a string or character literal is written with one, two or three hex digits, so how many characters it consumes depends on the character that happens to come next.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `VariableLengthStringHexEscapeSequence` (`resharper_variable_length_string_hex_escape_sequence_highlighting`) |

## Why

`\x` is the only escape in C# whose length is not fixed: the compiler takes up to four hex digits, and it does not stop at the ones the author meant. `"\x41B"` is one character, U+041B — not `A` followed by `B`. Append a letter to a string that ends in `\x41` and its last character silently changes; the diff shows one character added and the program changed two. ⚠ **`\u` has a fixed length of four and cannot do this**, which is why the fix is a spelling change and nothing else. ⚠ **The other two inspections this concept was drawn from are not here, and both were measured out.** `1l` is `CS0078` — "the 'l' suffix is easily confused with the digit '1'" — on by default, and a probe confirms it fires on `1l` and on `1lu` and stays quiet on `1ul`. A `char` argument widening to an `int` parameter is a different question about overload resolution, not about how a literal reads, and it is not this rule.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var cyrillic = "\x41B";
```

Write:

```csharp
var cyrillic = "\u041B";
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Only the spellings where the length is genuinely undecided are reported**: a `\x` followed by exactly four hex digits has consumed all it can and reads as one thing, so it is left alone. One, two or three digits are reported whatever follows them — including at the end of a literal, where nothing follows — because the hazard is that the next edit decides the value, not that the current text is already wrong. ⚠ **A verbatim literal has no escapes and neither does a raw string literal**, and both are skipped by the token kind rather than by scanning: `@"\x41B"` is six characters and reporting it would be reporting text that does not mean what the rule assumes. ⚠ **`\\x41B` is a backslash followed by `x41B` and is not an escape**, so the scanner consumes both characters of every `\\` before looking for the next one; a rule that searched for the two-character string `\x` would report it. Interpolated strings are scanned segment by segment through their text tokens, so the expressions inside the holes are never mistaken for literal text. The fix rewrites `\xH`, `\xHH` and `\xHHH` to the `\u` form with the digits zero-padded to four, which is the same character by construction and is why it is safe to apply without review. Generated code is excluded.
